title: Chebyshev is Fourier — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of Chebyshev is Fourier's rich face, its first round at Sketch tier, a proposal: three walks, each up to a test of its section's claim (the browser's lookup table driven past its ends, Chebyshev's points against Runge, a wallpaper group's rules on the torus grid), with the fingerprint of the words each was laid against. The circle's shadow, Dissolutions' proof of the identity, waits for its own way up; a later round can gather it once that lands. What the tests found waits below as offers. I never hold the entry's words.

offers.what: The identity sentence holds as written: a full-width cosine through Tₙ gives harmonic n alone (through a 4097-point table every other harmonic sits below −100 dB, and the browser's own WaveShaperNode agrees with that table to 1.6e-7). The next sentence, 'a weighted sum of Chebyshev polynomials is a waveshaper whose output harmonics are its coefficients', needs the same condition and doesn't state it. Measured: at drive a, Tₙ's own harmonic comes out at aⁿ and the rest spills into lower harmonics of its parity (T₃ at a = 0.50: h1 = −1.125, h3 = 0.125). A saw built this way misses its drawbars by 6.6% of the loudest at a = 0.99 (−23.6 dB) and by 42% at a = 0.90, where harmonics 4 to 6 are nearly gone; above 1 the table holds its end values and puts about −17 dB of the power above its top drawbar. The rule below 1 was found first on the paused Dissolutions branch claude/dissolutions-sequences-905758 (its circle's shadow sequence, steps 6 and 7, T₃ at reach 0.6); this run measured the same thing again and adds the saw figures and the held ends. For even n the spill also includes a steady offset (harmonic 0). The challenger's independent recomputation agreed. Proposed: '…whose output harmonics are its coefficients when it is driven at full scale; drive it softer and the spectrum moves with the drive.'

'Often terrible far away (Runge's phenomenon)' gives Taylor's failure the wrong name. Runge's phenomenon is what a polynomial through evenly spaced points does at the ends; Taylor's series of the same curve, 1/(1 + 25x²), fails because it adds up only within 1/5 of its centre, the distance to the curve's poles at ±i/5. Measured in the nodes piece: Taylor at 0 converges inside |x| ≤ 0.15 (worst gap 3.6e-2 at degree 8, 6.4e-5 at degree 30) and diverges at x = 0.25 (3.6 at degree 8, 490 at degree 30), while interpolation at evenly spaced points passes a worst gap of 1 at n = 9 and reaches 60 at n = 21, and at the shadow points falls to 1.5e-2. Proposed: '…often terrible far away (past its radius of convergence; Runge's phenomenon is the related failure of fitting through evenly spaced points).'

offers.section: Spending it back into the torus
offers.what: 'The group zeroes out the rest' holds for some groups only. On the 7 × 7 grid of cos(mφ₁)·cos(nφ₂), measured: cmm zeroes 24 modes (m + n odd) and ties none; p4m zeroes none and ties 21 pairs across the diagonal (aₘₙ = aₙₘ), leaving 28 of 49 free; p4g zeroes 27 and ties 9 pairs, 3 of them with a sign flip. Every projected surface holds its group's moves to 4e-15 and breaks the next move up. The cosine-times-cosine basis also has both axis mirrors built in (flip error exactly 0 for any weights), so a quarter turn asked for without mirrors comes out as p4m or p4g. Reasoned from that, not measured group by group: this basis reaches only the four groups with mirrors in two perpendicular directions on a square cell (pmm, cmm, p4m, p4g). Of the other thirteen, eight (p1, p2, pm, pg, cm, pmg, pgg, p4) need sine terms on a square torus, and five (the three- and six-fold groups) need a lattice no square torus has, sines or not. Zero-or-tie is a fact about the cos × cos basis, not the group: in a basis of symmetric and antisymmetric pairs, p4m zeroes 21 combinations. The subspace sentence stands. Proposed: 'the group zeroes some modes and ties others in pairs', and a clause that this cosine basis reaches pmm, cmm, p4m and p4g only.

verdicts.file: Chebyshev is Fourier — rich — the drive.html
verdicts.why: Tests the sentence and walks up well, but steps 3–5 and its 'Where this leads' box retrace the claimed, paused Circle's Shadow sequence on claude/dissolutions-sequences-905758 (any Tₙ, the summed curve, the reach below 1, the same proof at the end). Remake to the part only it has: keep steps 1–4 (rewrite step 3's Try in its own words), make the test the real WaveShaperNode driven from 1.00 upward, where the held ends put power above the top drawbar that no polynomial can, and drop the below-1 range, the T₃ spill equation and the box.

A true test, honestly captioned, but Loudon sent it back as the end of a proof and paused its own way up, still claimed; gathering it here with another walk named as its way up answers his note a second time unasked. Remove the manifest entry only — the Dissolutions file is not this face's and stays untouched; gather the landed sequence with it in a later round.

pieces.file: Chebyshev is Fourier — rich — the drive.html
pieces.title: The drive · a waveshaper built from Chebyshev tables
pieces.caption:
**Harmonic design by lookup table, and what the table does past its ends.** Five steps: a 110 Hz cosine through a straight table, then through T₂ for one octave, then any Tₙ for the nth harmonic, then one table summed from eight drawbars, its harmonics measured off the browser's own WaveShaperNode: at a drive of 1 the drawbars are the spectrum. Last, the drive pushed from 1 upward. The drawbars' polynomial has degree 8 and can make nothing above the 8th harmonic at any drive; the browser's table holds its end values instead, and at a drive of 1.10 about −17 dB of the power lands above the top drawbar.

table(x) = table(±1) for |x| > 1

(the browser's table, read past its ends) = (the value at the nearest end)

pieces.title: Nodes on the circle · the points that beat Runge
pieces.caption:
**Equal steps round a circle, dropped to the line, and what they do for a polynomial.** Four steps: a point going round and its shadow, n equal steps whose shadows bunch at the ends (the roots of Tₙ), a polynomial through n evenly spaced points that flies off at the ends, and then the test: the same curve through the shadows' points. At n = 21 the worst gap is 60 through evenly spaced points and 0.015 through the shadows'. Taylor's series at the middle rides along as a third reading, to show its failure is a different one. Silent.

xₖ = cos((2k + 1)π ⁄ 2n)

(shadow point k) = the cosine of (equal step k round the half circle)

verdicts.file: Chebyshev is Fourier — rich — selection rules.html
verdicts.why: A test that disagreed with the text and says so: counts recomputed by group averaging (cmm 24 zeroed; p4m 21 tied; p4g 27 zeroed, 9 tied, 3 signed). Note: the zero-or-tie split belongs to the cos×cos basis, not the group; a line saying so would keep 'p4m zeroes nothing' from reading as a fact about p4m.

pieces.file: Chebyshev is Fourier — rich — selection rules.html
pieces.title: Selection rules · which modes a symmetry lets a torus surface keep
pieces.caption:
**Ask the torus for a wallpaper group, and count what it does to the cosine grid.** Four steps: one mode cos φ₁ · cos φ₂, heard as two tones when two phases scan it; a 7 × 7 grid of modes; one symmetry move and what it does to each mode; then the test. cmm zeroes every mode with m + n odd, and at a scan ratio of 1 the note jumps an octave. p4m zeroes nothing and ties each cell to its mirror across the diagonal. p4g does both, some ties with a sign. A quarter turn without mirrors can't be had: the basis brought its mirrors with it.

W(g · φ) = W(φ) for every move g in the group

(the surface after any of the group's moves) = (the surface)
